topics.topic: Backup cryptographic format, authenticated-encryption construction, key handling, and confidentiality scope
questions: What exact cryptographic construction and versioned backup format implement encryption, authentication and the key digest?
Which authenticated-encryption construction, nonce generation, key derivation or key-size rule, file authentication, and key-digest algorithm and representation must a backup use?
Which authenticated-encryption construction, nonce generation, key interpretation or derivation, authentication scope and key-digest algorithm are required?
Does “cannot be read” mean only that the encrypted store contents cannot be read, while the declared metadata remains readable, or must no part of the backup be readable without the key?

judgement.why: This asks the same backup-encryption and versioned-format question as P2, and the relevant texts have not changed.

precedent.topic: Backup encryption, nonce, key identifier, authenticated metadata, and container format
quotes: Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
precedent.why: The algorithm, nonce, authenticated envelope, key identifier and cryptographic-version representation are encoding and file-format contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Backup filename, prefix, collision, and unencrypted-record format and validity rules
questions: What makes an unencrypted backup record valid for scheduling, retention deletion and display as the newest backup?
Must the kept and temporary prefix match sets be disjoint, and how is that enforced?
When the destination kept name already exists, which file is preserved and which is removed?
What are the exact prefixes, timestamp precision and filename encoding, and the syntax and validation rules of the unencrypted backup record that governs scheduling, display, retention and deletion?

Is this unencrypted record cryptographically authenticated, and if so how can Registry authenticate it before choosing a key; if not, may corrupted or altered metadata control retention, newest-backup display and integrity checks?
What are the two prefixes, the instant's filename representation and precision, and the complete rule for producing a unique kept name when two runs record the same instant?

quotes:
It
   records, readable without its key, its instant, the release that made it,
   the last audit sequence number it holds and a digest of the key it was
   made with (never the key); its age is counted from that instant.

Kept and temporary names begin with two different prefixes the release
   declares; Registry removes, renames and deletes in the backup location
   only files under them, and the location is Registry's alone (A17): a file
   is under a prefix when it is a regular file directly in the location whose
   name begins with it; Registry follows no link and enters no directory
   there.

A kept
   name is made from the backup's instant and is never overwritten: a backup
   whose kept name exists, or whose rename fails, is deleted and the run
   fails.

The process looks at the clock at least once a minute; a date's
   run starts at its first look at or after 03:00 of that date when an
   earlier look of the same process saw that date before 03:00, and no kept
   backup of that date exists — a kept backup's date being the UTC date of
   its recorded instant, and a file whose record cannot be read counting as
   none (rule 4), so
   a restart, a start at 03:00 or a clock set back makes no second run.

Third, whatever the second step did, it deletes every kept
   backup made more than 30 × 24 hours before, and every file under the kept
   prefix whose unencrypted record (rule 1) cannot be read.
judgement.divergence: One careful implementation can use overlapping prefix match sets, treat merely parseable metadata as valid, and delete the new candidate on a kept-name collision; another can require disjoint prefixes, validate metadata against the encrypted payload, and interpret the collision deletion differently. The owner notices through kept backups being preserved, deleted, displayed, or considered for scheduling and retention differently.
judgement.why: Although exact filename and record encodings belong to State 6, the texts leave consequential cleanup, collision, prefix-membership and metadata-validity behaviour open.

topics.topic: Configuration variable names and item-specific well-formedness rules
questions: What exact forms are accepted or refused for the store location, backup location, backup key, owner credential and service tokens?

What are the exact environment-variable names and lexical formats for the store location, backup location, backup key, owner credential, and four service tokens, and what precisely makes each item malformed?
What are the exact environment-variable names for every listed item, including the four service tokens, and which names are reserved or recognized as unknown?
Beyond the later path and length rules, what exact conditions make each configuration item well formed, and how is the byte length of an environment string measured?

judgement.why: This is the same configuration-variable naming and item-specific well-formedness question as P3, on unchanged text.

precedent.topic: Exact configuration variable names, encodings, syntax, and value validation
quotes:
The configuration is the set of environment variables whose names begin
   with `REGISTRY_`, set as R0-23 says; no other variable is read or
   checked.

It holds exactly these items and no other: the store's
   location; the backup location and the backup key (A18); the owner
   credential; one service token for each service of A09 — PresuPro, Client
   Portal, Cabinet, Cabinet Kernel (R0-20, R0-23) — or, for an owner-only
   start, none of the four: Registry then serves the owner interface alone
   and refuses every service call (A18 rule 9).
precedent.why: Exact environment-variable names, value encodings, path syntax and structural validity rules are configuration-schema and encoding details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Outcome when decrypted-backup or failed-candidate cleanup fails during backup checking
questions: Does failure to remove the decrypted temporary file prevent keeping an otherwise valid backup, what artifacts remain, and which failure is reported?

If checking succeeds but removal of the decrypted temporary file fails, or cleanup of a failed candidate fails, is the encrypted backup kept, deleted, or left temporary, and does retention step three still run?

If the decrypted copy passes its checks but cannot be removed, is the encrypted backup still renamed and kept, or is the second step failed and the encrypted temporary backup deleted or left for the next run?

quotes:
Second, it
   writes the backup under a temporary name and checks it: it decrypts it
   into a second temporary file, opens that for reading only, checks that it
   is the store version of its release, that the store's own integrity check
   passes and that its audit log ends at the recorded sequence number, and
   removes it; a backup that passes is renamed to its kept name, one that
   fails is deleted.

Third, whatever the second step did, it deletes every kept
   backup made more than 30 × 24 hours before, and every file under the kept
   prefix whose unencrypted record (rule 1) cannot be read.

A step that fails leaves no partial kept backup —
   at most a file under the temporary prefix, which the next run removes —
   and writes a diagnostic that names the failure and no value (A17);
   Registry keeps serving, and the next 03:00 tries again.
judgement.divergence: One implementation keeps and renames an otherwise valid encrypted backup despite failure to remove its decrypted temporary copy; another treats that cleanup failure as failure of the check and deletes or leaves the encrypted candidate temporary. The owner notices whether a checked backup is kept and what files and diagnostic remain.
judgement.why: The second step does not define the result when validation succeeds but cleanup fails, or when deletion of a failed candidate also fails.

topics.topic: Session-validity and locking rules for requests racing sign-out or expiry
questions: How does the sweep synchronize its expiry check and upload removal with admitted requests, sign-out, and updates of the session’s last-request instant?

If an uploaded-file request passes the session check before sign-out but sign-out acquires the import and session locks first, must the earlier request still run before sign-out, be refused after sign-out, or be allowed to run against the ended session?

If an upload or other file request passes the session check but a sign-out or expiry ends the session before it acquires both locks, is it still allowed to run and recreate state in the ended session, or must session validity be checked again under the session lock?

judgement.why: This is the same question as P11 about an admitted uploaded-file request racing sign-out, and the quoted locking and admission rules have not changed.

precedent.topic: Whether admitted upload or confirmation requests survive concurrent sign-out
quotes:
A sign-out is applied in turn with the session's other requests that
   change it: one admitted before it completes its change to the store, and
   leaves nothing in the ended session.
precedent.why: A request admitted before sign-out completes its store change even if it acquires the session lock later, while no state remains in the ended session.

topics.topic: Atomicity, rollback, and recovery for partially created stores after failed startup
questions: Which files and mutations must be undone after each possible startup failure, especially a partially created new store?
Must creation and initialization of a new store be atomic, and what must the next start do if the process or filesystem fails after creating the file but before initialization is complete?

quotes:
A failed start leaves no
   file it made but a probe it could not remove, which the next start or run
   removes with the other temporary files.

When the store's
   configured file does not exist and its directory does, Registry makes a new,
   empty store of the running release's version there at the start; otherwise
   the store must open for reading and writing and carry the store
   version of the running release, and a store of another version, or one
   that does not open, fails the start — bringing a store to a new version is
   a step of the release, not of the start.
judgement.divergence: One implementation creates the store atomically and removes every incomplete candidate after failure; another leaves a partially created store that the next start attempts to open and consequently refuses. The owner notices whether the next start succeeds or requires manual repair.
judgement.why: The texts require a failed start to leave no created file but do not define an atomic creation or recovery rule for interruption or partial initialization.

topics.topic: Encoding, byte-length, normalization, and equality rules for secrets
questions: Which encoding or decoding defines a secret’s byte length and equality, and are secrets raw text, hexadecimal, base64, or another representation?

How are environment-variable strings converted to bytes for the 32-byte test and constant-time comparison, and is distinctness tested on the supplied text, decoded bytes, or a normalized representation?

judgement.why: This asks the same canonical encoding, byte-counting and equality question for configured secrets as P8, with no relevant text change.

precedent.topic: Canonical encoding used to measure, compare, and distinguish configured secrets
quotes:
A secret — each token, the owner credential and the backup key — is at
   least 32 bytes long; a shorter one fails the start.

A presented secret is compared in constant time; no secret enters a record,
   a log line, an audit entry, a diagnostic or an answer (R0-23, R0-37).
precedent.why: The textual or binary representation, decoding, equality and byte-counting rules for credential fields are encoding and contract details owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Meaning and enforceability of the one-minute expired-upload cleanup bound
questions: Is one minute a hard bound on removal, a bound on sweep-start attempts, or only a target when the lock and process are healthy?

How is the one-minute maximum guaranteed when an upload, mapping, confirmation or import may hold or wait for the import lock without any duration, fairness or priority bound, and an already-admitted upload may acquire the lock after the session ends?

quotes:
An uploaded file is changed only by a holder of the import lock: an
   accepted import, holding it, drops every session's upload; the upload of
   a session ended by its limits is dropped by a sweep that takes the import
   lock at least once a minute, so it stays in memory at most a minute after
   the session ends, reachable by no request.

Uploads
   and every other request that reads or changes an uploaded file — showing
   the mapping or the import's confirmation step, confirming, a sign-out —
   take the instance's one import lock first, then their session's lock
   (A13), check the closure while holding them, and hold both until done; when the closure exists, uploading, showing the mapping or the import's
   confirmation step and confirming are refused, and a sign-out goes on.

Registry bounds neither how long a run takes nor how
   old the newest kept backup may be.
judgement.divergence: One implementation treats one minute as a hard deletion deadline and prioritizes or bounds the sweep's lock acquisition; another merely attempts the sweep once per minute and permits an upload to remain longer while the lock is occupied. The owner or host administrator notices the different duration for which personal data remains in process memory.
judgement.why: The asserted one-minute retention bound has no rule limiting import-lock wait or hold time, so careful implementations cannot enforce the same observable cleanup behaviour.

topics.topic: Scope of the instance-wide import lock across requests and owner sessions
questions: Which requests may a request holding the instance-wide import lock block, and what does “other requests are not held by them” exclude?
May a request in one owner session block uploaded-file requests in other sessions on the instance-wide import lock, or does the promise that other requests are not held exclude that?

quotes:
The requests of one owner session that change its state — showing a
   confirmation step, uploading a file, a submission, a sign-out — are
   applied one at a time, in the order in which they take the session's one
   lock, after passing the session check — those that read or change an
   uploaded file take the import lock before it (A16 rule 2): each sees the
   session as the one before left it, and other requests are not held by
   them, so a confirmation
   bound to a file a later upload replaced is refused (A16 rule 2).

Uploads
   and every other request that reads or changes an uploaded file — showing
   the mapping or the import's confirmation step, confirming, a sign-out —
   take the instance's one import lock first, then their session's lock
   (A13), check the closure while holding them, and hold both until done; when the closure exists, uploading, showing the mapping or the import's
   confirmation step and confirming are refused, and a sign-out goes on.

Other
   session changes take their session's lock alone.
judgement.why: The instance-wide import lock serializes every request that reads or changes an uploaded file across sessions, while unrelated requests take no import lock and therefore are not held by it.

topics.topic: State and uploaded-file reclamation when an owner session expires
questions: Does the same sweep remove the entire expired OwnerSession, including its pending confirmation and CSRF state, or only its uploaded file; and when is the remaining runtime state reclaimed?
Does an uploaded file cease to exist immediately when its session expires, as M11 and the first sentence require, or may it remain in memory until a later sweep?

quotes: Everything in it ends with the session.

An uploaded file is changed only by a holder of the import lock: an
   accepted import, holding it, drops every session's upload; the upload of
   a session ended by its limits is dropped by a sweep that takes the import
   lock at least once a minute, so it stays in memory at most a minute after
   the session ends, reachable by no request.
judgement.why: All OwnerSession state ends logically with the session, while the text expressly permits the inaccessible bytes of an uploaded file to remain in memory until the sweep removes them, for at most one minute under the stated rule.

topics.topic: Whether the four service tokens are required or optional in owner-only mode
questions: During the presence check, exactly when are the four token items optional as a group, and which missing-token combinations fail?
Does the presence check require the four token variables in owner-only mode, and if so must they be absent, present empty, or represented by an explicit mode value?

judgement.why: This is the same all-four-versus-none token-presence question answered by P4, and the relevant configuration rules have not changed.

precedent.topic: Validation of all-token versus token-free owner-only configuration
quotes:
It holds exactly these items and no other: the store's
   location; the backup location and the backup key (A18); the owner
   credential; one service token for each service of A09 — PresuPro, Client
   Portal, Cabinet, Cabinet Kernel (R0-20, R0-23) — or, for an owner-only
   start, none of the four: Registry then serves the owner interface alone
   and refuses every service call (A18 rule 9).

A configuration with some service tokens but without Client Portal's
   stops the start and names the missing item; one with none of the four is
   an owner-only start.
precedent.why: The texts expressly permit none of the four tokens for owner-only mode and reject a partial token set.

topics.topic: Backup scheduling behavior after a forward clock jump past the daily run time
questions: If the clock jumps from a prior date or from before midnight directly to a later date after 03:00, should that later date run even though the process never observed that same date before 03:00?

topics.topic: Canonical digest algorithms, encodings, framing, and ordering for imports and confirmations
questions: Which digest algorithm, byte encoding, field framing and canonical ordering define the file digest and the confirmation-input digest, including absent values and nested picks?

topics.topic: Collision handling for customer references minted during import
questions: What happens if a minted `customer_ref` collides with an existing Customer or with another Customer minted in the same import?

topics.topic: Meaning and validation of the audit sequence recorded in a backup
questions: Is the recorded value the store's never-reused sequence counter or the highest surviving AuditEntry, and what value and check apply to a new store whose audit log has no entries?

topics.topic: Ordering of upload validation versus import-closure checks
questions: When the import is closed and an upload is also too large, unreadable, or otherwise invalid, is it refused for closure immediately, or does A04's global order require value validation before the lifecycle/closure check?

topics.topic: Startup cleanup requirements for temporary backup files and probes
questions: Must startup remove backup temporary-prefix files and leftover probes, at which point in the ordered checks, and does a cleanup failure stop startup?
